title: If you're struggling to get feedback because your game uses AI heavily, I am happy to give feedback
author: NostalgicBear
selftext:
Disclaimer up front : I reference my Discord server in the post.


I've been in game dev in some regard for the past 10 years (released a few games, and worked on various others).  We all know the game dev landscape is changing (arguably for better and for worse in some regards), and in time, games made with heavy AI involvement will undoubtedly become more accepted over time.


I run a Discord server that is currently (mostly) focused on playtesting indie games, specifically ones where developers have struggled to get concrete feedback. The whole idea is to try and give feedback to those that are struggling to get it. A number of devs in the server rely heavily on AI (code, art, brainstorming, everything). They dont hide it, and its clear to see. One of the overwhelming pieces of feedback I've received from that subset of developers is that they found it extremely difficult to get people to playtest their game, because a judgement is made the moment a player sees that first bit of AI art at the main menu, or the moment they are met with an obvious Claude UI. This is a crying shame, because some of the best games I have played since starting the server clearly involve heavy use of AI, but my God, have they been fun. Yes, there will always be slop, but slop existed pre-2022 as well. 


I had my reservations when it came to predominantly AI developed games, and had I not started playtesting indie games earlier this year, I probably wouldn’t have given many of these games the chance they deserved. I'm happy to admit when I was wrong. Not only have I now had a chance to play some really interesting games, I’ve had a chance to have some great conversations with the developers behind them, and its been so enjoyable and rewarding to have conversations with people passionate about bringing their game to life, irrespective of the tools used to do so.


I feel like its breathed new life into me when it comes to just being in the realm of indie games, as I was feeling exhausted from the constant negativity of reverse engineering, excessive clones of games, constant arguments over AI etc.


I appreciate its a nuanced topic, but it's been brilliant to see people that wouldn't have been able to bring their ideas to life, get a chance to do so now.


I’m no Indie Game Joe. I can't put your game in front of thousands of people, but if you are struggling to get people to give it a chance, I can play it and give you feedback as best I can. If any of you are in the same boat, where you're finding it difficult to get feedback, please consider dropping into the server  (Link in bio. Not including here as to not break sub rules)

comments.author: thvaz
comments.body:
I would really appreciate a playtest of Submundus.

It’s a dungeon crawler with deckbuilding and survival, where your deck represents your body, inventory, and time. Wounds, hunger, and exhaustion become cards. I’m developing it soloand mostly with no budget, using AI-assisted tools, including for some visuals and audio.

The free demo is currently in Steam Next Fest. It’s getting some wishlists, but very few people are playing, and I have limited feedback on the opening experience.

I’d especially appreciate your first impressions: where things become confusing or tedious, and whether you feel like continuing after the first 10–15 minutes. If you stop, knowing where and why would be very useful.

[https://store.steampowered.com/app/5273910/Submundus\_Demo/](https://store.steampowered.com/app/5273910/Submundus_Demo/)

Thanks for offering this!

replies.author: NostalgicBear
replies.body:
Im going to keep feedback light on this thread as there are a lot to answer.


Gameplay


- I played 3 battles and won all 3 pretty easily. I only lost one party member on one occasion.
- I used Banshee, Salamander and Strigoi, along with two other summons.
- During battles, there's very little time to read or digest what's happening, so the combat didn't really capture my interest or help me understand what was going on.
- When a battle finished, I had no idea what I'd done right or wrong, so I didn't come away feeling like I'd learned anything.
- Battles lasting over a minute feel quite long, although I think this is largely because it's so difficult to follow what's happening with text constantly appearing and disappearing on screen.
- I did think the battle animations were quite nicely done.


UI


- There's quite an awful lot of UI presented immediately. It feels overwhelming.
- The tutorial is quite odd. You show me the board with Leshy, explain things through a few popups, and then take me back to the main menu rather than letting me actually use what you've just taught me.
- It's not made very clear that items need to be applied.
- You're trying to fit too much text onto the individual summon cards when hovering over them.
- Some of the font sizes are far too small. If you want anyone over 35 to comfortably read the battle statistics, I'd strongly consider increasing them, eg the text "Each combat turn advances both teams’ meters and status durations. Playback changes viewing speed. Support casts specials only." was barely legible.
- I tabbed away from the game during a battle, and when I returned, the game had paused. The PLAY button was very difficult to see because it was grey against a grey background, due to the background art at that moment.


Art


- I liked the parallax effect on the main menu.
- I'm not sure the art really complements the battles. I almost wonder whether the game would look better with more minimal art.
- It's not that the art is bad, but it sometimes feels like clutter. I'd rather be able to see the actual character icons more clearly.
- I think a more minimalist use of art would actually be better here. I think the art is too much and that you should focus on character cards rather than the background art.
- The battle animations themselves are nicely done.
